title: II. The Injured Foot
paragraphs: The first of these tasks was at Madame Hohlakov's house, and he hurried there to get it over with quickly and not be too late for Mitya. Madame Hohlakov had been slightly unwell for the past three weeks: her foot had swollen up for some reason, and though she wasn't confined to bed, she spent the day half-reclining on the couch in her boudoir, in a charming but proper state of undress. Alyosha had once noted, with innocent amusement, that despite her illness Madame Hohlakov had started dressing rather more elaborately — top-knots, ribbons, loose wrappers had all made their appearance — and he had a suspicion why, though he dismissed the idea as frivolous. Over the last two months, the young official Perhotin had become a regular visitor to the house.

Alyosha hadn't called in four days, and he was in a hurry to go straight to Lise, since it was with her he needed to speak — Lise had sent a maid to him the day before, specifically asking him to come see her "about something very important," a request which, for certain reasons, interested Alyosha a great deal. But while the maid went to announce him to Lise, Madame Hohlakov learned of his arrival from someone and at once sent to beg him to come see her "just for one minute." Alyosha decided it would be better to grant the mother's request, or else she'd keep sending down to Lise's room every minute he was there. Madame Hohlakov was lying on the couch. She was dressed with particular smartness and was clearly in a state of extreme nervous excitement. She greeted Alyosha with cries of delight.

"It's been ages, ages, absolute ages since I've seen you! A whole week — just think of it! Ah, but you were here only four days ago, on Wednesday. You've come to see Lise. I'm sure you meant to slip into her room on tiptoe without my hearing. My dear, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, if only you knew how worried I am about her! But more of that later — though that's really the most important thing, more of that later. Dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, I trust you completely with my Lise. Since Father Zossima's death — God rest his soul!" (she crossed herself) — "I look on you as a monk, though you look charming in your new suit. Where did you find such a tailor around here? No, no, that's not the main thing — more of that later. Forgive me for calling you Alyosha sometimes — an old woman like me can take liberties," she smiled coquettishly; "but that will keep too. The important thing is that I shouldn't forget what's important. Please remind me yourself. The moment my tongue runs away with me, just say, 'the important thing?' Ach! How am I supposed to know now what's most important? Ever since Lise took back her promise — her childish promise, Alexey Fyodorovitch — to marry you, you've realized, of course, that it was only the playful fancy of a sick child, who'd been stuck in her chair so long — thank God she can walk now!... that new doctor Katya sent for from Moscow, for your unfortunate brother, who tomorrow — But why talk about tomorrow? I'm ready to die at the very thought of tomorrow. Ready to die of curiosity.... That doctor was with us yesterday and saw Lise.... I paid him fifty roubles for the visit. But that's not the point, not the point again. You see, I'm mixing everything up. I'm in such a hurry. Why am I in such a hurry? I don't understand it. It's awful how I seem to be losing the ability to understand anything. Everything seems tangled up in a knot. I'm afraid you're so bored you'll jump up and run off, and that'll be the last I see of you. Goodness! Why are we sitting here with no coffee? Yulia, Glafira, coffee!"
Alyosha hurried to thank her, saying he'd only just had coffee.
"Where?"
"At Agrafena Alexandrovna's."

"At ... at that woman's? Ah, it's she who's brought ruin on everyone. Though I know nothing about it, really. They say she's turned into a saint, though it's a bit late in the day for that. She'd have done better to start sooner. What use is it now? Hush, hush, Alexey Fyodorovitch, I've so much to tell you that I'm afraid I'll end up telling you nothing at all. This awful trial ... I shall certainly go, I'm making arrangements. I'll be carried there in my chair — besides, I can sit up. I'll have people with me. And, you know, I'm a witness. How shall I speak, how shall I speak? I don't know what I'll say. One has to take an oath, doesn't one?"
"Yes; but I don't think you'll be able to go."

"I can sit up. Ah, you're putting me off! Ah, this trial, this savage business, and then everyone's off to Siberia, some are getting married, and it's all happening so fast, so fast, everything's changing, and in the end — nothing. Everyone grows old and has death to look forward to. Well, so be it! I'm tired. This Katya, _cette charmante personne_, has dashed all my hopes. Now she's going to follow one of your brothers to Siberia, and your other brother's going to follow her, and live in the nearest town, and they'll all torment each other. It drives me out of my mind. Worst of all — the publicity. The story's been repeated a million times in every paper in Moscow and Petersburg. Ah, yes, would you believe it, there's a paragraph saying I was a 'dear friend' of your brother's — I can't even repeat the horrid word. Just imagine, just imagine!"
"Impossible! Where was this paragraph? What did it say?"

"I'll show you right now. I got the paper and read it yesterday. Here, in the Petersburg paper, _Gossip_. It only started publishing this year. I'm terribly fond of gossip, so I subscribe — and now look what it's done to me, that's what gossip comes to! Here it is, right here, this passage. Read it."
And she handed Alyosha a sheet of newspaper that had been tucked under her pillow.

It wasn't exactly that she was upset — she seemed overwhelmed, and perhaps everything really had become tangled in her head. The paragraph was very typical, and must have come as quite a shock to her, but, fortunately perhaps, she couldn't fix her mind on any one subject for long, and so might dash off to something else entirely the next minute and forget the newspaper altogether.

Alyosha was well aware that news of the dreadful case had spread across all of Russia. And, heavens, what wild rumors he'd read over those two months, about his brother, about the Karamazovs, about himself too, among other equally credible items! One paper had even claimed he'd entered a monastery and become a monk, in horror at his brother's crime. Another contradicted this, and reported that he and his elder, Father Zossima, had broken open the monastery's strongbox and "made a run for it." This particular paragraph, in the paper _Gossip_, ran under the headline "The Karamazov Case at Skotoprigonyevsk." (That, alas, was the name of our little town, which I've kept concealed until now.) It was brief, and Madame Hohlakov wasn't named directly in it. No names appeared at all, in fact. It simply stated that the criminal, whose upcoming trial was causing such a sensation — a retired army captain, idle and swaggering, reactionary and bullying by nature — had been continually entangled in amorous intrigues, particularly popular with certain ladies "pining away in solitude." One such lady, a grieving widow trying to pass for young despite a grown daughter, had been so taken with him that a mere two hours before the crime she'd offered him three thousand roubles on condition he elope with her to the gold mines. But the criminal, counting on escaping punishment, had chosen instead to murder his father for the three thousand rather than go off to Siberia on the strength of his pining lady's middle-aged charms. This playful little item wrapped up, naturally, with an outburst of noble indignation at the horror of parricide, and at the lately abolished institution of serfdom. Reading it with curiosity, Alyosha folded the paper and handed it back to Madame Hohlakov.

"Well, that must be me," she rushed on again. "Of course it's me they mean. Barely an hour before, I'd suggested the gold mines to him, and here they go on about 'middle-aged charms' as though that were my motive! He wrote it out of spite! God Almighty forgive him for the middle-aged charms, just as I forgive him! You know it's — do you know who wrote it? It's your friend Rakitin."
"Perhaps," said Alyosha, "though I haven't heard anything about it."
"It's him, it's him! No 'perhaps' about it. You know I threw him out of the house.... You know the whole story, don't you?"
"I know you asked him not to come see you anymore, but why, I haven't heard ... from you, at least."
"Ah, then you've heard it from him! He abuses me, I suppose, abuses me dreadfully?"
"Yes, he does; but then he abuses everyone. But why you turned him out I haven't heard from him either. I hardly see him these days, in fact. We're not friends."

"Well, then, I'll tell you the whole thing. There's no help for it — I'll admit there's one small point where I was maybe to blame. Only a tiny, tiny point, so small it probably doesn't even count. You see, my dear boy" — Madame Hohlakov suddenly looked coy, an enigmatic, charming smile playing on her lips — "you see, I suspect ... You must forgive me, Alyosha. I'm like a mother to you.... No, no, quite the opposite. I'm speaking to you now as though you were my father — mother's entirely the wrong word here. Well, it's as though I were confessing to Father Zossima, that's exactly it. I called you a monk just now. Well, that poor young man, your friend Rakitin (mercy on us, I can't stay angry with him — I'm cross, but not very), that frivolous young man, would you believe it, seems to have gotten it into his head to fall in love with me. I only noticed it later. At first — a month ago — he just started calling more often, almost every day, though of course we already knew each other before. I had no idea ... and then suddenly it dawned on me, and I began noticing things, to my surprise. You know, two months ago, that modest, charming, excellent young man Pyotr Ilyitch Perhotin, who's in the service here, started coming regularly to the house. You've met him here yourself, ever so many times. And he's an excellent, earnest young man, isn't he? He comes once every three days, not every day — though I'd be glad to see him daily — and always so well dressed. On the whole, I love young people, Alyosha, talented, modest ones, like you, and he's got almost the mind of a statesman, he talks so charmingly, and I'll certainly, certainly try to get him a promotion. He's a future diplomat. On that awful day he very nearly saved me from death, coming in the middle of the night. And your friend Rakitin comes in such boots, and always stretches his legs right out on the carpet.... He started hinting at his feelings, in fact, and one day, as he was leaving, he squeezed my hand terribly hard. My foot started swelling right after he pressed my hand like that. He'd met Pyotr Ilyitch here before, and would you believe it, he's always sniping at him, growling at him, for some reason. I just watched the two of them go on and laughed to myself. So I was sitting here alone — no, I was laid up then. Well, I was lying here alone and suddenly Rakitin comes in, and just imagine, brings me some verses of his own composition — a short poem, about my bad foot: that is, he described my foot in a poem. Wait a moment — how did it go?
A captivating little foot.

It started something like that. I can never remember poetry. I've got it somewhere — I'll show it to you later. But it's a charming thing — charming; and, you know, it's not only about the foot, it had a good moral too, a charming idea, only I've forgotten it — really, it was just the thing for an album. So, of course, I thanked him, and he was clearly flattered. I'd barely had time to thank him when in comes Pyotr Ilyitch, and Rakitin's face turned as black as night. I could see Pyotr Ilyitch was in the way, because Rakitin obviously had something more to say after giving me the verses. I sensed it, but Pyotr Ilyitch walked in regardless. I showed Pyotr Ilyitch the verses without saying who wrote them. But I'm convinced he guessed, though he won't admit it to this day, and insists he had no idea. But he says that on purpose. Pyotr Ilyitch started laughing right away and picking it apart. 'Wretched doggerel,' he called it, 'some divinity student must have written it' — with such vehemence, such vehemence! Then, instead of laughing, your friend flew into a rage. 'Good gracious,' I thought, 'they'll be at each other's throats.' 'I wrote it,' he said. 'I wrote it as a joke,' he said, 'because I think it's degrading to write verses.... But they're good poetry. They want to build a monument to your Pushkin for writing about women's feet, while I wrote mine with a moral purpose, and you,' he said, 'are an advocate of serfdom. You've got no humane ideas,' he said. 'You're untouched by enlightenment, uninfluenced by progress, you're a mere official,' he said, 'and you take bribes.' Then I started screaming and begging them to stop. And, you know, Pyotr Ilyitch is anything but a coward. He at once took the most gentlemanly tone, looked at him sarcastically, listened, and apologized. 'I had no idea,' he said. 'I wouldn't have said it if I'd known. I'd have praised it instead. Poets are all so touchy,' he said. In short, he was laughing at him under cover of the most gentlemanly manner. He explained to me afterward that the whole thing had been sarcastic. I thought he meant it seriously. All the while I lay there, just as I'm lying now, in front of you, wondering, 'Would it be proper, or wouldn't it, for me to throw Rakitin out for shouting so rudely at a guest in my house?' And, would you believe it, I lay here with my eyes shut, wondering whether it would be proper or not. I fretted and fretted, my heart started pounding, and I couldn't decide whether to make a scene or not. One voice seemed to say, 'Speak,' and the other, 'No, don't speak.' And no sooner had the second voice said that than I cried out and fainted. Of course, there was a fuss. I got up suddenly and told Rakitin, 'It pains me to say this, but I don't wish to see you in my house again.' So I threw him out. Ah! Alexey Fyodorovitch, I know myself I did wrong. I was putting it on. I wasn't really angry with him at all; but I suddenly imagined — that's what did it — that it would make such a fine scene.... And yet, believe me, it was all quite genuine too, because I really did cry, for several days afterward, and then all at once, one afternoon, I forgot all about it. So it's been a fortnight since he was here, and I kept wondering whether he'd come again. I wondered even yesterday, and then suddenly last night this _Gossip_ turned up. I read it and gasped. Who could have written it? He must have. He went home, sat down, wrote it on the spot, sent it off, and they printed it. That was a fortnight ago, you see. But, Alyosha, it's dreadful how I keep talking and never say what I mean to say! Ah! The words just come pouring out on their own!"
"It's very important for me to get to my brother in time today," Alyosha faltered.
"To be sure, to be sure! You bring it all back to me. Listen, what's an aberration?"
"What aberration?" asked Alyosha, puzzled.
"In the legal sense. An aberration where everything's forgivable. Whatever you do, you're acquitted on the spot."
"What do you mean?"

"I'll tell you. This Katya ... Ah, she's a charming, charming creature, only I can never work out who it is she's in love with. She was here not long ago and I couldn't get a thing out of her. Especially since she won't talk to me now except on the surface. She's always going on about my health and nothing else, and she's taken such a tone with me, too. I just told myself, 'Well, so be it, I don't care'.... Oh, yes, I was talking about aberration. This doctor's come, you know. You know a doctor's come? Of course you do — the one who finds madmen. You wrote to him. No, it wasn't you, it was Katya. It's all Katya's doing. Well, you see, a man may be sitting there perfectly sane and suddenly have an aberration. He can be conscious, know exactly what he's doing, and still be in a state of aberration. And there's no doubt Dmitri Fyodorovitch was suffering from aberration. They discovered aberration the moment the law courts were reformed. It's all thanks to the reformed courts. The doctor was here, and questioned me about that evening, about the gold mines. 'How did he seem then?' he asked me. He must have been in a state of aberration. He came in shouting, 'Money, money, three thousand! Give me three thousand!' and then went off and murdered him right away. 'I don't want to murder him,' he said, and then he went and murdered him anyway. That's why they'll acquit him — because he fought against it and still murdered him."
"But he didn't murder him," Alyosha broke in, rather sharply. He felt more and more sick with worry and impatience.
"Yes, I know — it was that old man Grigory who murdered him."
"Grigory?" Alyosha cried.
"Yes, yes, it was Grigory. He lay there where Dmitri Fyodorovitch struck him down, then got up, saw the door open, went in, and killed Fyodor Pavlovitch."
"But why, why?"

"Aberration. Once he came to from the blow Dmitri Fyodorovitch gave him on the head, he was in a state of aberration, and went and committed the murder. As for his saying he didn't do it — very likely he just doesn't remember. Only, you know, it'd be much better, ever so much better, if it turns out Dmitri Fyodorovitch murdered him. And that's how it must have been, even though I say it was Grigory. It certainly was Dmitri Fyodorovitch, and that's better, ever so much better! Oh, not better that a son should have killed his father, I don't defend that — children ought to honor their parents — and yet it would be better if it were him, since then you'd have nothing to cry over, because he did it while unconscious, or rather, while conscious but not knowing what he was doing. Let them acquit him — that's so humane, and it would show what a blessing the reformed courts are. I knew nothing about any of this, but they say it's been going on a long time. And when I heard about it yesterday I was so struck that I wanted to send for you at once. And if he's acquitted, have him come straight from the courthouse to dinner with me, and I'll have a party of friends over, and we'll drink to the reformed courts. I don't believe he'd be dangerous — besides, I'll invite a great many friends, so he could always be led out if he tried anything. And afterward he might be made a justice of the peace somewhere, or something, in another town, because people who've had their own troubles make the best judges. And besides, who isn't suffering from aberration nowadays? You, me, all of us are in a state of aberration, and there are countless examples of it — a man sits singing a song, suddenly something annoys him, he grabs a pistol and shoots the first person he comes across, and no one blames him for it. I read about that recently, and every doctor confirms it. Doctors are always confirming things — they'll confirm anything. Why, my Lise is in a state of aberration. She made me cry again yesterday, and the day before too, and today I suddenly realized it's all due to aberration. Oh, Lise grieves me so! I believe she's quite mad. Why did she send for you? Did she send for you, or did you come of your own accord?"
"Yes, she sent for me, and I'm just on my way to her." Alyosha got up, resolute.

"Oh, my dear, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, maybe that's the most important thing after all," Madame Hohlakov cried, suddenly bursting into tears. "God knows I trust Lise to you with all my heart, and it doesn't matter in the least that she sent for you on the sly, without telling her mother. But forgive me, I can't trust my daughter quite so easily to your brother Ivan Fyodorovitch, though I still consider him the most chivalrous young man. But just imagine, he's been to see Lise and I knew nothing about it!"
"How? What? When?" Alyosha was thoroughly astonished. He hadn't sat back down, and listened standing.

"I'll tell you — that's perhaps why I asked you to come, since I don't even know now why I asked you to. Well, Ivan Fyodorovitch has been to see me twice since he got back from Moscow. The first time he came as a friend, to call on me, and the second time Katya was here, and he came because he'd heard she was here. I didn't, of course, expect him to visit often, knowing how much he already has on his plate — _vous comprenez, cette affaire et la mort terrible de votre papa_. But then I suddenly heard he'd been here again — not to see me, but to see Lise. That was six days ago now. He came, stayed five minutes, and left. And I didn't hear about it until three days later, from Glafira, so it was a real shock to me. I sent for Lise right away. She laughed. 'He thought you were asleep,' she said, 'and came in to ask after your health.' So that's how it happened, of course. But Lise, Lise, mercy on us, how she torments me! Would you believe it, one night, four days ago, right after your last visit, once you'd gone, she suddenly had a fit — screaming, shrieking, hysterics! Why is it I never have hysterics? Then, the next day, another fit, and the same thing the day after, and yesterday too, and then yesterday, that aberration. She suddenly screamed out, 'I hate Ivan Fyodorovitch! I insist you never let him into the house again.' I was struck dumb by these astonishing words, and answered, 'On what grounds could I refuse to see such an excellent young man, a man of such learning too, and so unfortunate?' — because this whole business is a misfortune, isn't it? She suddenly burst out laughing at my words, and so rudely, you know. Well, I was pleased — I thought I'd amused her and the fits would pass, especially since I wanted to stop seeing Ivan Fyodorovitch anyway, on account of these strange visits without my knowledge, and meant to ask him for an explanation. But early this morning Lise woke up and flew into a rage at Yulia and, would you believe it, slapped her across the face. That's monstrous — I'm always polite to my servants. And an hour later she was hugging Yulia's feet and kissing them. She sent word that she wasn't coming to see me at all, and would never come see me again, and when I dragged myself down to her, she rushed to kiss me, crying, and while kissing me, pushed me out of the room without a word, so I couldn't find out what the matter was. Now, dear Alexey Fyodorovitch, I'm pinning all my hopes on you, and, of course, my whole life is in your hands. I simply beg you to go to Lise and get everything out of her, as only you can, and come back and tell me — me, her mother — because you understand it will be the death of me, simply the death of me, if this goes on, or else I'll run away. I have patience, but I might lose it, and then ... then something awful will happen. Ah, dear me! At last, Pyotr Ilyitch!" Madame Hohlakov cried, beaming all over as she saw Perhotin walk in. "You're late, you're late! Well, sit down, speak, put us out of our suspense. What does the lawyer say? Where are you off to, Alexey Fyodorovitch?"
"To Lise."
"Oh, yes. You won't forget, will you, what I asked you? It's a matter of life and death!"
"Of course I won't forget, if I can ... but I'm so late," Alyosha muttered, making a hasty retreat.
"No, be sure, be sure to come back — don't say 'if I can.' I'll die if you don't," Madame Hohlakov called after him, but Alyosha had already left the room.
